title: Student Grants
subtitle: Build the school-year funding stack before accepting the loan balance

blocks.text: Tuition is one number. School somehow adds books, bus fare, groceries and a laptop charger that disappears precisely during midterms.

Canada Student Grants are student aid you do not pay back. You apply through the province or territory where you live for good. One application usually checks you for both grants and loans, federal and provincial. The amount depends on your need, your course load, your program and school, your family income and things like having children or a disability.
For the 2026–27 school year, the Canada Student Grant for Full-Time Students pays up to $4,200 a year, or $525 for each month of study. “Up to” depends on your need and income.

items.title: “I apply to the federal government separately for each Canada Student Grant.”
items.text: Most students send one provincial or territorial student aid application and are checked for federal and local aid in it. The grants prefer a coordinated entrance.

blocks.text: Knowing which school money you never pay back lets you borrow less and finish with a smaller debt.
blocks.detail: Four kinds of money can land in the same account, and only one expects to be repaid on its own terms.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you label every dollar.

sections.title: Give Every Dollar the Right Label

blocks.text: Four kinds of money can land in the same account. Only one of them expects to be repaid on its own terms.

items.title: GRANT
items.text: Usually not paid back if you still qualify and stay enrolled. Getting too much, or a change in your status, can still mean paying some back.

items.title: LOAN
items.text: Borrowed student aid that you must pay back. Federal Canada Student Loans have no interest, but you still have to repay them, and the provincial part has its own rules.

items.title: SCHOLARSHIP OR BURSARY
items.text: Money from your school, community, employer or a private group, with its own rules about grades, need, reports and renewal.

items.title: WORK AND SAVINGS
items.text: Job income, RESP withdrawals, family help and savings can change your budget and sometimes your aid. Declare what the application asks for.

blocks.text: For 2026–27, the part-time student grant is up to $2,520 a year and cannot be more than your assessed need. Part-time status follows student aid rules, not your opinion of a busy Tuesday.
The Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Quebec run their own student aid systems instead of Canada Student Grants and Loans. Apply through the right one.

items.title: “A grant can never be converted into money owing.”
items.text: Dropping out, a change in course load, not confirming you are enrolled or a new review can turn part of a grant into a loan or an overpayment. “Not paid back” assumes your file stays accurate.

sections.title: One Application Can Ask About Several Grants

blocks.text: Students with children, students with disabilities and part-time students may get extra help. Fill in the right part of the application and send the papers it asks for. Do not assume the basic grant covers everything.

items.title: HELP FOR EACH CHILD OR DEPENDANT
items.text: Full-time students who qualify may get up to $2,240 a year for each dependant, on top of the full-time grant.

items.title: STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES
items.text: The Canada Student Grant for Students with Disabilities is $2,800 a year. A separate grant for services and equipment may pay back approved school costs, up to its limit.

blocks.text: After you are assessed, compare the total aid with your real budget for the school year. Money may come in parts after your school confirms you are enrolled. Do not spend a grant twice just because the provincial site and NSLSC both show it.

items.title: “The assessment amount is guaranteed until graduation.”
items.text: Aid is reviewed every school year and can change with your income, program, course load, family or policy. Reapply and update your file each year.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: apply early through the right province or territory, tell them about everything that applies, keep grants and loans apart, and compare your confirmed aid with your full school-year budget before you borrow more.

sections.title: Mina and the Grant That Appeared Twice

paragraphs: Mina Tran starts nursing school in Winnipeg. Her goal is to finish without a pile of debt, so she plans her eight months down to the dollar: rent, food, the bus and her hospital placements.

She logs in to her provincial student aid account and sees a federal grant and a loan. Then she logs in to NSLSC and sees the same kind of money again. Mina briefly believes the grant has duplicated itself out of academic enthusiasm.
She is tempted to plan around both totals. There is a used laptop she needs, and a deposit for a better room near the hospital. With double the money, she could say yes to both.
Before she spends a dollar, Mina decides to check the money in three places: her award letter, her school account and her bank. It takes one evening and a lot of tea.
The truth is simple. Both screens show the same award. Tuition goes straight to the school first, and only the rest reaches her bank. Her budget had counted every number it saw as new money.
There is one good surprise. Her application asked about disability, and she had skipped it. She sends the papers in, and a disability grant covers the laptop.
Her funding does not shrink. Her double-counting does. Mina ends up with one grant, one loan, one laptop and one budget that knows the difference.

blocks.text: Match your aid in three places: the assessment letter, your school account and your bank deposit. Timing and tuition payments can make one award look like several different amounts.
One award can show up on two screens without doubling. Match the letter, school account and deposit before you budget a single dollar twice.
Mina avoided spending her grant twice, and found a disability grant she had missed, by checking three places.
blocks.detail: Matching your award letter, school account and bank deposit can protect your own budget all year.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): School-Year Funding Stack and Gap Plan

blocks.text: Use rounded numbers and short labels. Do not write student numbers, bank details or logins here.

Full-time student aid usually has a lifetime limit of 340 weeks, with different limits for doctoral students and students with disabilities. Keep track of how many weeks you have used, not just this year’s award.

items.title: Assessed need
items.text: Your school costs minus the money you are expected to have, under aid rules.

items.title: Grant
items.text: Student aid you usually do not pay back if you keep meeting the rules.

items.title: Student loan
items.text: Borrowed aid that you must pay back.

items.title: Study period
items.text: The dates used to work out your costs and aid.

items.title: Enrolment confirmation
items.text: Your school’s proof that you are enrolled, which releases your funds.

items.title: Overaward
items.text: Aid above what you now qualify for, which you may have to pay back.

quiz.question: True or False: “I apply to the federal government separately for each Canada Student Grant.”

questions: Which province or territory do you live in, and when is your application deadline?
Which school and program are you in, and are you full time or part time?
Do you have children or a disability that the application should know about? (Yes / No / Not sure)
About how much grant money and loan money were you approved for this year? Estimates are fine.
About how much will school and living cost you this year? Round to the nearest hundred if that is easier.
What is one thing you will check before you borrow more?
samples: Nursing at a college in Winnipeg, full time.
Yes. I have a learning disability.
About $4,200 in grants and $6,000 in loans.
Whether the grant on both websites is the same money.
